segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Do you remember how to say "to call"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You need to open the association between "to call" and "to phone" and "to call myself", "my name is", and then you remember it.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llamar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Llamar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now we can look a little bit at how the line in the past and the dot in the past interact.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, we do this in some very common structures in both languages. For example,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you might say something like, "I was cooking when the phone rang."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I was cooking when the phone rang." Which part is the line and which part is the point?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: "I was cooking" is the line.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: "The phone rang" is the dot.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, let's begin with "I was cooking". What is "to cook"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cocinar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cocinar. Good. "I was cooking"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cocinaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "When"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuánto...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cuando.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "The phone rang". El teléfono is "the phone", like in English, which is actually from Greek.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This first bit "tele-" means "far, distant" and "-phone" means "voice". So, it's the "distant voice" is the telephone.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "when the phone rang", and we will say "when the phone sounded". And "to sound" is sonar. Sonar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "when the phone sounded"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando el teléfono sonó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: All together, "I was cooking when the phone rang". Not from memory, but thinking it through again. "I was cooking when the phone rang".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cocinaba cuando el teléfono sonó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Cocinaba cuando el teléfono sonó, or cocinaba cuando sonó el teléfono, which would probably be more natural order in Spanish:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: cocinaba cuando sonó el teléfono.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But both orders are perfectly fine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To arrive" was llegar, llegar, "to arrive".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And this is double L, so we have the double L which is like a Y sound, e-g-a-r, -ar verb, llegar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I arrived"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegué.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llegué.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "He arrived"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llegó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "We arrived"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llegamos. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I was speaking on the phone when María arrived."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we're not going to say literally "on the phone" in Spanish. We will say por, por teléfono, "by phone". Por can also mean "by".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I was speaking on the phone when María arrived"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaba por teléfono cuando María llegó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Hablaba por teléfono cuando María llegó or hablaba por teléfono cuando llegó María, either way. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we can see how we're using the line and the point together.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you was to look up "to stay" in the dictionary, you would find quedarse.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Then you need to do something with that se. So, if you wanted to say "I stayed", how would it be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me quedé.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me quedé.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "He stayed", or "she stayed", or "you formal stayed", "it stayed"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se quedó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se quedó. And "we stayed"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nos quedamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nos quedamos, which of course could also mean "we stay" or "we are staying". Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to please", the verb that we use to express "like"? "To please"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Gustar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Gustar. Good. And if you want to say "I like it", you say "it pleases me". So, how do you say "I like it"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me gusto. Me lo gusto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We're working on intuition now. We've got "me" and "it" and we're throwing it all in there, but we must...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sorry, me gusta.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, we must process it literally. "It pleases me." "It pleases" — gusta. "It pleases me" — me gusta. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if you want to say "I liked it", you just say, of course, "it pleased me". So, how would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me gusté. Sorry, me me gustó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me gustó. Good. Me gusté, what does that mean? Me gusté?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: "I pleased myself."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I liked myself." Me gustó, "it pleased me", "I liked it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I didn't like it"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No me gustó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No me gustó. "I didn't like it. It didn't please me."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Apart from the point in the past, you could also use the line in the past here, depending on the context.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, how would you say that? "It wasn't pleasing me."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No me gustaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No me gustaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, with this line and point we're not looking for direct translations from English. We are looking to understand the concept

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: of the line in time and the point in time and applying it directly in Spanish. Because in English you would never say something like, "I wasn't liking it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And a lot of the time it's totally interchangeable in Spanish. No me gustó, no me gustaba just means you're thinking in a different way when you say it. No me gustó,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you're referring to something as an event, as something closed.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And no me gustaba, you're thinking about something as an ongoing thing that occurred over a period of time. Really, a lot of the time that difference between the point and the line in time just originates in the mind.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Parecer, parecer was "to seem", parecer.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Parecer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's related to "apparent", and we have aparecer in Spanish which means "to appear".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is "transparent" similar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Transparent" also is related. Yes, of course. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, parecer is "to seem". How would you say "it seems to me", "it seems to me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me parece.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "It seems good to me", or in Spanish, "it seems well to me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me parece bien.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me parece bien. How would you say "it seemed good to me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me parecí...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "It seemed".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, yes, of course. Me pareció bien.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me pareció bien, "it seemed good to me". And you might want to use the line in the past. You might want to say like "it was seeming good to me".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, even though this is not a translation you would use in English, in Spanish you're just thinking about, "Do I mean a point in time or do I mean ongoing in this context?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we might want, "It was seeming to me well." How would you say that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Parecer becomes parecía. Me parecía bien.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me parecía bien. "It seemed good to me, but when I saw it I didn't like it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "it seemed good to me" (it was seeming good to me)?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me parecía bien,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "but"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: pero

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "when I saw it"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: cuánto... cuando lo vi,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I didn't like it"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: no me gustó.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Me parecía bien, pero cuando lo vi no me gustó. And again here we see the interaction, no, between the line and the point.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me parecía bien, "it was seeming okay, fine to me", pero cuando lo vi, "but when I saw it" — this is a very clear point in the past —

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I didn't like it". In that moment when I saw it, I didn't like it. Again, the point in the past. Me parecía bien, pero cuando lo vi no me gustó. Excellent.
